newsitem.title: USA: Treasury's Hawke raises U.S. bank reform concerns.
newsitem.headline: Treasury's Hawke raises U.S. bank reform concerns.

text.p: A top U.S. Treasury official urged Congress on Thursday to enact broad financial reform legislation, but raised numerous concerns about the bill in its current form.
"There are compelling reasons to enact legislation this year -- but not at any price," Treasury Undersecretary John Hawke told a House Commerce Committee subpanel.

The bill approved by the House Banking Committee includes provisions that create an uneven playing field among financial industries and that fail to remove some barriers to competition, Hawke said in prepared testimony.

"Insurance sales provisions in the bill would curtail competition and discriminate against national banks," Hawke said. The bill would retain existing rules limiting many national banks sales of insurance in towns with more than 5,000 people, he said.

Hawke also objected to a part of the bill giving an umbrella regulator authority to impose capital requirements on securities and insurance firms that own banks. Such companies "would be subject to potentially burdensome new capital regulation," he said.
Hawke also said bank-issued securities should be subject to Securities and Exchange Commission oversight, not bank regulators.

And a provision to create so-called wholesale financial institutions, which would accept uninsured deposits, failed to provide adequate safeguards to protect the financial system, taxpayers and consumers, Hawke said.
Despite the objections, Hawke said financial reform was urgently needed.

"We believe Congress has the best opportunity it has had in many years to enact historic and long-overdue legislation benefitting American consumers and strengthening our nation's financial system," he said.
The Commerce Committee has until mid-September to complete its work on the bank reform bill, which was passed narrowly by the House Banking Committee last month.

Even if the committee approves a bill, the legislation faces an uncertain fate. Congress has been trying for more than a decade without success to reform the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act and overhaul financial regulations.
